Abstruse

ab-STROOS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Abstruse is difficult to understand because of its complexity or depth.

The footnotes in the philosophy textbook were often more abstruse than the chapters they were explaining.

Worked Example

The professor's abstruse lecture on quantum entanglement left most of the class taking notes they didn't understand.

Abstruse fits genuinely deep, technical material -- not something merely long or boring, but something hard to grasp.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

impenetrable: Impenetrable writing shuts every reader out -- there is no way into it at all, however much effort or expertise you bring. Abstruse material is deep and demanding but not sealed shut: a specialist who works at it patiently does get through. Impenetrable admits no one; abstruse admits the persistent expert.

labyrinthine: Labyrinthine is about structure: an argument so winding, with so many branching turns, that you lose the path through it. Abstruse is about depth -- the ideas themselves are hard, however tidily they are arranged. A labyrinthine chapter confuses by its maze-like layout; an abstruse one by sheer difficulty.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

accessible: easy to understand or use

straightforward: uncomplicated and easy to follow

Where it sits · how hard it is to understand — technical → abstruse → unfathomable

technical vs. abstruse: Technical sits below abstruse: a technical manual's unfamiliar terms slow you down, but a motivated reader can usually work through it, while abstruse ideas stay hard even after every term is explained.

unfathomable vs. abstruse: Unfathomable goes beyond abstruse: an abstruse proof eventually yields to a specialist's patient effort, but something unfathomable is so far beyond understanding that even experts may never fully grasp it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — abs-

prefix — abs-: away, from (Latin ab-)

root — -truse

root — -truse: pushed, thrust (from trudere, "to push") (Latin trusus)

Put it together

Put it together: Abstruse comes from Latin abs- ("away") + trusus ("pushed") -- literally "pushed away, hidden" -- describing an idea shoved so far out of easy reach that most people can't get to it.

Use the root in a new word: protrude

Use the root in a new word: protrude: A single loose nail protruded from the old fence board, snagging every jacket that brushed past.

Word Choice

Abstruse describes the difficulty of a subject itself -- dense philosophy, advanced math -- rather than confusion caused by bad writing or unclear instructions.
